Labels!

Words are like thought-vehicles. They're supposed to take ideas from my head and carry them into your head. If the idea in your head is different than the idea in my head then that means the vehicle is broken. Broken words are kind of useless, and are often counter-productive.

Such is the fate of a lot of identity-labels. A good example is "feminist". If I said "Sally is a feminist", that means a whole lot of different things to a bunch of you out there. There's no guarantee that a single one of you has the same thought in your head as I have in mine. If I said "Johnny is a feminist", there's a lot of you that would reply "That's not even possible, men can't be feminists!" Thus completely missing that I was trying to communicate a thought to you, and not start a semantics debate about what the "proper" definition of a word is.

So what I want to try and do is bring about a call-to-arms. It would be great if everyone just agreed from now on that instead of involving yourselves in semantic debates, that instead you each make an attempt to try to have the same idea in your head as the person who is trying to communicate an idea to you has in their head. For some people this is easy, and for other people this can be quite difficult.

So instead of trying to correct someone's definition of a word, just try to adapt their usage for the time that you're talking to them. And if there's any confusion, try to get to a common definition by way of other words.

Instead of "feminist", you could say "a person who supports women's rights", or if you and the person you're talking to want to use different words, then use those. Another popular one popping up is "a person who supports equal rights among the genders." Those are two different definitions of "feminist", so when talking about things that require that distinction, why not just spell it out completely and stop using the label?

Maybe I'm wrong / crazy. Thoughts?
I'm a liberal, unless that means that you think I'm stupid. In that case, I'm a conservative, unless that means that you think I'm stupid.
Crazy. But that's okay. I prefer issues not labels myself

Interestingly both the words "fascist" and "feminist" has suffered the same fate. They don't really mean anything anymore in common use (at least here). Such a thing tends to happen to words as they become more controversial, but the main issue is that neither terms have owners. There's no one "feminist" group that owns the word and can tell you who is or is not a feminist, and the same with fascist. This is in contrast to words like 'republican' and 'democrat' where you can easily tell if a person is objectively and officially a part of their respective groups.
Until you successfully uncouple human emotion from reasoning, good luck separating a words connotation from its denotation.

This happens all the time in academic research, so you always have to start out defining your terms. As long as you do that, it doesn't matter what term you use.

Example: "In this presentation I will use the term 'Pasta primavera' to describe an individual for whom their tenets of faith are the first consideration in any life decision." Others might prefer 'religious person' or 'devotee' or 'person of faith,' but that part doesn't matter. It's the definition behind the term that's the key.

Define your terms and you'll be alright.

In discussion, I've found that - many times - arguments can be resolved by one participant halting the conversation, and say, "Let's step back, and define our terms." While disagreement over whether or not a particular term should be tied to a particular definition definitely occurs in those instances, things get a lot less heated and it's a lot easier to ferret out each person's thought processes, which can fast-track understanding others' positions - even if you don't agree, you can at least make sense of what they're saying.

We have a tendency to have a blind spot for our internal definitions of things, and unless we're specifically asked to explain them, don't really think about them and - I imagine - accidentally presume that others use the same definitions we do, which is rarely the case.

I think that, while there are reasonable steps that can be taken to minimize this, it's impossible to wholly circumvent.

We need labels in order to pack several complex ideas into one coherent sentence so that the latter can be expanded upon. The problems occur when people misconstrue the precise definition of labels. In the case of "liberal" and "conservative", all the former means is that someone is for reforming the current power structure, whereas the latter wishes to retain the status quo. Most Americans assume that anyone who is a "liberal" is pro-choice, anti-guns, and supports tax increases on the wealthy; however, "liberals" in China during Mao-Zedong's reign advocated for policies which rejected the tenets of communism.

Of course, the problem is deeper then that. George Lakoff wrote an excellent book entitled Moral Politics. Lakoff is a linguist by trade who researches the deepest depths of human communication. He theorizes that our conceptions of the words which construct social reality are prototypes, constituting the shortcuts necessary to make complex ideas possible. These prototypes are intimately rooted in our experiences. For example, the word "bird" likely conjures up an image of an animal capable of flight; however, we know that there are multiple exceptions to this (penguins, ostriches, etc.). Similarly, the labels we construct to identify ourselves and others are subconsciously shifted with experiences, both direct and indirect, which pervade our lives. Because of this, even when we spell out what we mean when we say the word "feminist" (or anything else, for that matter), our exact understanding of the term will always be somewhat different to anyone else's (though clearly, those with similar experiences will naturally be closer). All of this means that when we are attempting to communicate with one-another, we're often not talking about quite the same thing.

Of course, this logic does occasionally get taken too far and enter the realm of irrationality, as it does when the most militant "feminists" declare that men cannot possibly be feminists or have anything to contribute to the discourse. Communication is much like building a machine; an engineer can be very precise, but it is impossible to create an engine with perfect efficiency. Similarly, while we can never perfectly convey ideas, we can get very, very close. Even though it's imperfect, by working together we can still achieve great things.

This discussion reminds me of George Orwell's 'Politics and the English Language.' Sometimes, people use words that don't really mean anything like "liberal" or "conservative" or "feminist." They just want to appeal to people. Instead of adapting to fluid definitions of groups of people, people should stick to their ideas. Identifying with a group will inevitably lead to your ideas being lumped in with everyone else's, making true discussion impossible. We have to leave behind the labels in order to get anywhere, in my opinion.

I think you may be misunderstanding Hawking Radiation. I'll see if I can break this down in a way that is fairly easy to understand.

When you're talking about Hawking Radiation, you consider a pair of virtual particles, specifically a particle anti-particle pair. These particle pairs necessarily come into existence, due to quantum effects, at a time scale that is essentially too small to measure (hence the name virtual). All we have to determine their existence is the pressure they exert on two closely spaced objects in a vacuum (The Compton Effect). When these particles are created ON THE EVENT HORIZON of a black hole, there is a chance that the anti-particle immediately ends up on the inside of the black-hole while the particle soars off into space as Hawking Radiation. This basically makes the virtual particles real to an observer outside of the black hole. And to keep the total energy of the universe at zero, the positive energy of the radiation implies the anti-particle in the black hole has negative energy. This implies that the mass of the black hole dissipates.

This is a classic example of the conceptual explanation of a complex physical process being far to simplified to fully encompass the process; however, I believe the above explanation should explain why the black hole will dissipate, as long as it is not taking in mass (from stars and planets etc.)

The antiparticle never was outside the blackhole, but rather created on the event horizon. The only information we have to tell us that it exists is the corresponding particle that radiates out into space. So as soon as we see that particle, we know for a fact the mass of the black hole is already less. Something need not enter the singularity for it to be considered a part of the black hole, it only has to be within the event horizon.

Additionally, in the reference frame of the antiparticle it would take a finite amount of time to reach the singularity. (Same for a person, though you'd be ripped apart by stretching due to the insanely strong gravitational force before getting close.)
